en: Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhànrán of Pílíng during the Táng Dynasty.
This work explains the refutation of the provisional nature of conceptualization. First, the names of the conceptual afflictions are listed: it says, "They are also called the three poisons.

This is because among the four types of conceptual afflictions (*saṃyojana*), the four types of pride (*māna*) are subsumed under delusion (*moha*); therefore, they are simply referred to as "three. First, [the poison of] non-opposition...
Because it causes the two [extremes] to be non-habitual tendencies,
it is called "correct.
This traverses the three [stages], which refers to the downward counting.
The nine levels of the three realms constitute the category of the inferior grade.
There are four in the desire realm and three each in the two upper realms.
Since there is no aversion (*dveṣa*) in the upper realms, there are only ten [afflictions] across the three realms.
The six heavens of the desire realm and the hells and continents differ; however,
because they are all alike lands of distraction,
they are counted as only one.
The general principle regarding the convergence of the four dhyānas is likewise.
As for the formless realms (ārūpya), there are no physical locations; they are distinguished by way of birth into four types.
Regarding what are called the "nine grades" (navaprakāra):
By means of wisdom, one cuts off delusions; as wisdom becomes increasingly distinct, delusions gradually come to an end.
How could there not be nine stages?
In establishing the teachings and judging the fruits, they are briefly categorized as nine.
Just as the judgment of rebirth is based on the superiority or inferiority of one's practice—
far exceeding the nine grades—
it is also spoken of in broad terms to accommodate ordinary beings.
The phrase "all are capable of" clarifies the functional capacity of the delusions (*moha*).
In their unsevered state, each one is individually capable of providing the power to moisten and sustain rebirth;
however, once any given fruit has been severed and exhausted, they no longer arise.
Regarding the "seven-times-at-most" (saptakṛtvah-parama) of the first fruit,
this is distinguished from the "view-attainer" (dṛṣṭiprāpta). Because they reach a maximum of seven births and never an eighth,
they are called "seven-times-at-most."
It is not necessary for all to reach the seventh [birth].
Thus, the third fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"Those of inferior capacity reach the seventh; those of middling capacity, the fifth or third; while those of superior capacity enter parinirvāṇa immediately upon birth."
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra* states:
"Within seven lifetimes, untainted wisdom reaches maturity;
it is like the method of taking medicinal butter, whereby the illness is eliminated within seven days."
Just as the *kalala* and other embryonic stages undergo a transformation every seven days;
just as the laws of kinship extend to the seventh generation;
and just as a seven-step snake travels for only seven paces due to its four great powers.
Due to the power of the snake's venom, it does not reach eight paces;
due to the power of delusion, it reaches seven, but the power of the Path does not reach eight.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says:
One should say fourteen; why then do you say seven?
Answer:
When counting the intermediate existence (antarābhava) and the fundamental existence (mūlabhava), the number does not exceed seven.
Therefore, it is simply called "seven.
Furthermore, because humans and the six heavens are born in seven places;
and because one cultivates the seven paths and abandons the seven fetters (anuśaya).
Regarding the seven messengers:
first, sensual desire; second, ill will; third, craving for existence; fourth, pride; fifth, ignorance; sixth, views; and seventh, doubt.
Furthermore, this is a general discussion on birth.
It should be stated that there are seven persons and seven heavens;
with fourteen intermediate states (antarābhava),
this totals twenty-eight births.
Furthermore, based on what was previously stated, since nothing more than seven [factors] emerge,
it is simply said that there are seven.
It is like a lamp that is at its brightest precisely when it is about to go out.
As previously cited from the *Suyāma-sūtra* in the *Zuìzìyì* (Following One’s Own Intent):
although one may possess desire and so forth,
through the power of the precepts associated with the Path (*mārga-samprayukta-śīla*), one is by nature free from sexual misconduct.
He commits no offense regarding the wives of others or his own wife at all times,
because he also abstains from improper times, improper places, and so forth even with his own wife.
Insects always naturally avoid him by a distance of four inches.
Having already severed the delusions of views, one attains the wisdom of the selflessness of persons;
although there may still be instances of independent mental factors or associated states within phenomenal objects,
one realizes that all phenomena arise from conditions and does not reckon them as having an intrinsic nature or reality.
Because it is free from perversion regarding the three poisons, it is called "right.
Although it can moisten rebirth, it does not invite the four miserable destinies;
this differs from the lower [level], which excludes the delusions of views.
Seeing this, one understands that the mind of attachment arises in accordance with its objects;
because it can create the causes for the four miserable destinies,
the three poisons remain present within the bodies of noble ones who are still bound by all fetters.
Not only does it not act as a cause for the four realms of existence,
but its arising is also free from both attachment and aversion;
therefore, it is unlike views that give rise to pervasive clinging.
The phrase "called 'contemplative'" explains the name by way of its lower [category].
This affliction can only be severed through intensive deliberation and contemplation.
Therefore, it is called "contemplation" (saṃkalpa).
The following section clarifies the similarities and differences between the two schools.
Regarding the *Abhidharmakośa* (Treatise on Establishment) challenging the Sautrāntikas:
First, it is difficult to maintain that greed for what is superior and craving for what is inferior are distinct opposites.
Next, if one argues that they are distinct only in name but identical in meaning,
then one should not differentiate between greed and craving based on their relative weight.
Regarding the term "concomitant" (*sahagata*):
according to that master’s treatise, one should further take ill-will (*vyāpāda*) as its concomitant.
Since in the higher realms, subtle greed (*parīttarāga*) is designated as "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*), [the same logic applies here].
Why is it that light anger in the higher realms is called *pratigha* (ill-will),
yet it is said that *pratigha* does not operate in the higher realms? Therefore,
in the "Chapter on Latent Proclivities" (*Anuśaya-nirdeśa*) of the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*, it says:
The seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are also listed as previously enumerated,
with the sole modification that the first is renamed "greed" (*rāga*).
These seven underlying tendencies, when distinguished by realm (*dhātu*) and mode of activity (*carita*), total ninety-eight.
The two underlying tendencies (anuśaya) of greed and hatred are each divided into five types according to realm and category.

That is to say, because there is one [tendency] for each of the five categories within the desire realm, greed does not extend upward; however, when distinguished by realm and category, there are ten [types of] craving.

This means that for each of the five categories within the two upper realms, there are five types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which do not extend downward; furthermore, when categorized by pride (*māna*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) according to their respective realms, there are fifteen types in total.
This is because there is one type for each of the five categories within the three realms.
There are five types of fetters of views,
namely the five [wrong] views.
When categorized according to the four truths, there are twelve in total.
That is to say: under the category of suffering, there are five;
for each of origination and cessation, there is one;
and under the category of the path, there are three.
Taken together, there are twelve;
across the three realms, there are thirty-six.
Regarding doubt concerning each of the Four Truths, there is one for each, totaling twelve across the three realms.
This results in a total of ninety-eight [afflictions],
clarifying that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) does not mutually interpenetrate between the upper and lower realms;
thus, the masters of the treatises raise difficulties regarding both cases.
However, the Buddha occasionally condescends to harmonize with [the views of others].
He merely intends to clarify the meaning behind the establishment of these names, so that one may recognize the objects of cognition;
what need is there for the hardship of contentious debate?
The citation of the analogy, the presentation of the root treatise, and the conclusion of its essential intent are all as stated in the text.
Second, regarding the clarification of the essence and contemplation:
since "emptiness" encompasses both analytical and essential [emptiness], it is necessary to list them.
The refutation of views is likewise so, as it is the beginning of the Mahāyāna gate.
Now, to further clarify the function of the analytical gate,
it is shown that both its beginning and its end are analytical.
The preceding discussion was for the purpose of distinguishing [the categories]; it is not the primary application.
This is the initial heading within the correct exposition of the method of contemplation.
Regarding "desire-delusion" (*kāma-kleśa*) and below, there is first a general heading for each grade, and each possesses three types of provisional designations (*prajñapti*).
First, the establishment of the cause is explained:
the six desires of women are cited as external conditions, which,
in relation to the mind, constitute the cause.
The conceptualization of desire that arises is called "the produced phenomenon.
Regarding the six objects of desire,
see the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 21.
The *Śāstra* on the Nine Meditations states:
"These nine types [of meditations] can remedy the seven kinds of defiled desire of the practitioner."
First, there are some people who are attached to forms,
such as blue, yellow, red, and white. Second,
there are some people who, even if they do not attach to forms, [are still affected by them].
They merely become attached to physical appearance— fine skin, slender fingers, long eyes, and high eyebrows. Or thirdly,
there are those who do not attach themselves to physical appearance,
but rather to deportment— the manner of advancing and stopping, sitting and rising, walking and standing.
Regarding the term "postures": it refers to bowing, looking up, looking down,
bending, stretching, raising the eyebrows, blinking, drawing near, and stroking.
One who beautifies their appearance and is skilled in deportment;
or fourth, there may be someone who does not observe dignified demeanor,
but whose speech is soft, beautiful, eloquent, and swift, speaking according to the occasion.
It accords with the mind and follows its intent, being able to move the hearts of people.
Fifth, there are some who do not attach to these at all,
but instead attach only to fine, smooth, soft, supple, and tender skin.
In times of heat, the body is cool; in times of cold, the body is warm.
Sixth, there are some who do not wear any of the aforementioned items, but instead wear only human skin, whether that of a man or a woman.
Seventh: Suppose there is a person who, although having attained the six higher states of non-attachment, still lacks true liberation;
they renounce the five kinds of sensual pleasures esteemed by the world and follow along with death.
Regarding this, as for the seventh [category], the persons to whom one is attached:
since these have already been collectively sought among the six [types of] objects of attachment, we now set aside the collective and retain the specific; therefore, it is simply called "the six."
The treatment of the nine [consciousnesses] governing the seven is fully explained in the *Chanmen* (Dhyāna-gate).
These six [objects], extending downward to the manifestation of the characteristics of greed externally,
are precisely the dharmas produced by the aforementioned six [consciousnesses] in relation to the internal faculty of mind (*manas*).
The citation of the first fruit (srotāpanna) as an illustration and the subsequent illustration of the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) are as stated in the text.
Nanda’s practice of desire is as previously cited.
Regarding the "conceptions of desire" (*kāmasaṃjñā*) and so forth in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
This is because they wish to deeply guard against the faults of desire;
they do not even give rise to such thoughts, let alone engage in physical union.
As for what is called "the aspect of desire":
The *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"The six classes of beings who enjoy sensual desire [engage in misconduct] through sexual intercourse, embracing,
holding hands, laughing, and gazing."
Those dwelling on earth engage in sexual intercourse;
however, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven take the wind as their means of union.
In Yāma Heaven they embrace;
in Tuṣita Heaven they hold hands;
in Nirmāṇarati Heaven they gaze and smile.
Those in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations merely look; they do not even give rise to thoughts, let alone look or smile.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* distinguishes between the lightness and gravity of human desires in the four continents.
In this continent, they are most numerous and cannot be further counted;
in the eastern continent, they reach a maximum of twelve degrees, while in the middle and lower regions, they are ten;
in the western continent, they reach as many as seven or eight, while the fewest are four or five.
In the northern continent (Uttarakuru), the maximum number is five and the minimum is three or four;
there are also those who practice the holy life (brahmacarya).
Therefore, those with excessive desire do not surpass the animals.
On this continent, there are likewise those with few desires, up to those who practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Such are the various characteristics of coarse and subtle perceptions.
If one takes these as the basis, they clearly establish the cause.
Taking the moving faculty of mind (*manas*) from within the aforementioned six characteristics, this is that which is produced.
Regarding the phrase "that which brings about the performance of deeds" within the context of continuity: it refers to the functioning of the mind.
This is intended to prevent the internal continuity of active phenomena;
it does not mean that active phenomena already exist within that continuity.
It is a provisional designation based on the general understanding that [all things] are unreal.
Regarding the principle of reason:
if one recognizes even the mind arising in response to objects as being illusory and provisional,
how could one further calculate that through marriage and betrothal rites one can restore vigor and prolong life?
Twice a month, one should commune with the divine to nourish life.
Even the non-Buddhist practitioners of the West, in their pursuit of such concentrations as the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception,
eliminate all craving for the lower realms.

Moreover, when calculating this principle as the right path, one next correctly cultivates contemplation by inferring that [the self] is established as being "neither identical nor different" from the aggregates; in this regard, one first applies the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) as a precedent.
If one performs the contemplation by inferring from the perspective of the lower [aggregates],...
The four lines below [discuss] severing delusions and realizing the truth, thereby establishing the two kinds of emptiness:
the emptiness of the nature of desirelessness and the emptiness of the characteristics of the non-existent.
The lines below on "sharp faculties" conclude that there are two different modes of practice for those with sharp and dull faculties.
The two practices for those of sharp faculties are as explained above in the refutation of views.
A person of superior capacity enters the truth immediately upon completing the refutation of the view of existence;
however, even if they have not yet attained correspondence [with that truth], they must still employ the sixty-four rounds of practice.
From "Setting forth" (*shè*) downwards, the sixty-four sections are clarified.
If one is dull-witted, the subsequent section marks the continuity and demonstrates the method of contemplation,
following the principle of establishing the argument through causes (*hetu*).

Next, regarding the two kinds of emptiness within the four lines of verse: the absence of desire is emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and the absence of the four [marks] is emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
In the preceding refutation of views, the three provisional designations were refuted; here, each is respectively concluded with the two types of emptiness.
In this context, following each and every provisional designation,
there is likewise a conclusion regarding non-arising and the two kinds of emptiness;
though the phrasing differs, the meaning is the same.
The first section concludes by clarifying that the remaining sections also possess the three types of provisional designations (*prajñapti*),
following the same pattern as the first section.
Regarding the refutation of greed, the remaining latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are likewise treated by analogy.
The ninth grade concludes the refutation of universality through the realization of non-arising.
The following section provides a detailed analysis.
The initial question is as stated in the text.
In the response, it is clarified that the two treatises distinguish their categories based on the difference in the application of the Path; thus, the categories are not the same.
Therefore, it is said in the *Abhidharma-śāstra* regarding the origin of the composition of the treatise:
Question:
For what reason is it called Abhidharma?
Answer:
This is because it refers to that which has been analyzed and that which has not yet been analyzed.
It is the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*),
the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
In the various *khandakas* (sections) below, it is simply stated that "the two paths subdue and the two paths sever.
If one judges from the perspective of the lower [realms], the two paths are distinct.
Next, in the refutation of the volition of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the difference in the wisdom employed is first clarified.
That which is called "worldly wisdom" (laukikajñāna) relies on the six modes of practice— delight and aversion— within worldly dhyāna;
that which relies on the principle of the outflow-free (anāsrava) is termed "outflow-free wisdom" (anāsravajñāna).
The person liberated both ways attains both types of knowledge;
at the time of severing delusions, they employ whichever one is appropriate.
If one is a beginner, one distinguishes between the two obstacles of phenomena and their nature.
For example, when wishing to enter the first dhyāna,
if one still perceives objects such as the bedding and furnishings within the sphere of the desire realm,
this is called an "obstruction of things" (vastu-āvaraṇa).
The delusion of desire has not yet been eliminated, and the obstruction of one's nature still persists.
If this delusion is destroyed, one immediately gives rise to the first dhyāna;
it is the same for the second dhyāna.
If vitarka and vicāra have not yet been eliminated, one does not give rise to the intermediate [dhyāna].
Only when the afflictions of the first dhyāna are destroyed does one give rise to the second dhyāna.
The obstacles of the third and fourth [dhyānas] may be understood by analogy with this explanation.
Within the first dhyāna, the initial passage clarifies the signs of the arising of the first dhyāna;
the subsequent middle and lower sections clarify the signs of the afflictions within the first dhyāna;
and the following sections, beginning with "each category," clarify the signs of the three types of provisional existence within the first dhyāna.
If one does not employ the "descending clarification" to refute [the opponent's position],
then even using the "descending" method, there are sixty-four permutations.
Next, regarding the "clarification by means of the cause established" for those who have proceeded to the second dhyāna:
Furthermore, it takes the meditative essence of the lower stage as its cause;
this is explained by analogy with the first dhyāna through the principle of continuity and mutual dependence.
Regarding the third dhyāna, it is said that "this bliss is even difficult to attain."
When the sages and the disciples of the Buddha practice this dhyāna,
they possess the contemplation of the noble lineages within each stage; therefore,
relinquishment is easy for them.
Because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) give rise to craving for the various stages (*bhūmi*), it is difficult for them to relinquish [them].
The meditative attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) has been briefly explained up to the realm of dhyāna.
As for the five types of *anāgāmin*:
If it were named solely after the earth element, it would be called only the Fourth Dhyāna.
This dhyāna has nine locations;
five of these are abodes of noble ones (ārya-vihāra) and are named the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens.
The state of non-conception belongs exclusively to ordinary beings;
the [other] three types of cessation apply to both ordinary beings and noble ones.
As for those who include birth within the five categories:
However, because there are five stages of cultivation through the permeation of dhyāna,
while the nine concentrations of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* permeate all nine stages,
here it permeates only the stage of the fourth dhyāna.
Having first attained it through cultivation, one further causes many moments of uncontaminated [states] to arise in succession;
from this, many moments of contaminated [states] are induced,
and from these, again, many moments of uncontaminated [states] arise.
In this manner, they gradually decrease until finally there are two moments of untainted (anāsrava) consciousness;
immediately thereafter, they induce two moments of tainted (sāsrava) consciousness.
Immediately thereafter, two moments of untainted (anāsrava) thought arise again;
this is called the "perfuming of the preparatory application" (*prayoga-saṃskāra*) that brings about the characteristic of completion.
Next, there is only a single moment of untainted thought.
Next, there is again only one moment of outflow-tainted [consciousness],
immediately followed by the arising of one moment of outflow-free [consciousness];
this is called the "establishment of the root."
Therefore, the Abhidharmakośa states:
"It is accomplished by a single moment of intermingling.
As for the phrase "five distinctions":
That is to say: inferior, middling, superior, most superior, and supreme.
Each grade consists of three levels, and each subsequent grade includes those preceding it;
thus, the fifth grade comprises fifteen levels in total.
These five grades, in their respective order,
give rise to the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa) by means of three, six, nine, and so forth [repetitions].
As for the term "intermittent perfuming" (miśrā-vāsanā):
This refers to the case where there is an outflow-free state at the beginning and end, with an outflowing state in between;
because many moments of such [outflowing] states are perfumed together by the outflow-free state to become a single moment of the outflow-free,
it is called "intermediate perfuming" (jia xun).
Regarding the term "Five Heavens," it refers to Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha.
From this point upward, there is no longer any affliction or confusion.
The beginning of the absence of affliction receives the name "Without Affliction" (Avṛha).
Because one subdues the afflictions, it is called "Without Heat" (Atapa).
Because its fruition is easily manifested, it is called "Well-Manifested" (Sudṛśa).
Because its vision is pure and penetrating, it is called Sudarśana (Good Vision).
Because it is unsurpassed among all forms, it is called Akaniṣṭha (Ultimate Form).
Below these, each of the three dhyānas further contains three heavens.
If one follows the Sarvāstivāda school, there are only sixteen bases (*ṣoḍaśa-sthāna*).
Within the first dhyāna, the most exalted and superior place is designated as the Brahmā-rāja;
therefore, it is not established separately.
Next, regarding the refutation of the three types of form— namely, the resistant and so forth— within the formless realm:
when one desires to enter the sphere of infinite space from the fourth dhyāna,
one must necessarily employ skillful means to extinguish these three types of form.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 21, states:
"Regarding the three kinds of form:
first, that which is visible and resistant (*sanidarśana-sapratigha*)."
Second, invisible and resistant;
third, invisible and non-resistant.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
Having transcended all perceptions of form and, by the cessation of perceptions of sensory resistance,
not attending to perceptions of diversity,
one enters the sphere of infinite space.
Transcending all forms, one eliminates visible and resistant forms;
eliminating resistant forms, one eliminates invisible and resistant forms;
by not attending to various characteristics of form, one eliminates invisible and non-resistant forms.
All material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) consist of only eleven types;
that is, the five sense organs, the five sense objects, and a portion of the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
This "portion" refers to non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
The Abhidharma states:
"One is visible;
namely, matter (rūpa)."
There are ten that are resistant (sapratigha),
namely the five sense organs and their five objects.
If one speaks of the "unseen and resistant," [it refers to the same].
One should simply say: "The five faculties and four objects;
three are invisible and non-resistant, namely a small portion of the dharma-āyatana."
The twenty-first fascicle of the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra states:
"When the eye perceives the disintegration of forms, it is called 'transcending form.
When the five sense faculties perceive the disintegration of their objects, it is called 'transcending the resistant.'"
The remaining two types, along with the non-informative (avijñapti), are termed "defects" and "dissimilar characteristics.
These three kinds of form all exist within the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Because one intends to enter the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), these three are extinguished.
Now, in this context, it should be stated that [the object] consists of the eightfold form and so forth within the *vimokṣas*, *abhibhvāyatanas*, and *kṛtsnāyatanas*.
Although non-informative matter (*avijñaptirūpa*) is not among the objects transcended by the present contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), [it is nonetheless included].
When one attains the contemplation of emptiness, one must certainly be free from both manifest and unmanifest form (*vijñapti-avijñapti-rūpa*).
Furthermore, regarding visible and resistant objects (*sanidarśana-sapratigha*),
one should further clarify the meaning of the three types of resistance (*pratigha*).
This is not the primary intent here, and therefore it is not discussed.
The methods for extinguishing form are fully detailed in the *Chanmen* (Dhyāna-gate).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 19, states:

Question:
Within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), is there definitely form, or is there definitely no form?
This is fully explained as in the *Shiqian* (Explanatory Notes).
Furthermore, it was once heard that there was a bhikṣu who, having attained the formless absorptions (ārūpya-samādhi), reached out into empty space upon emerging from concentration.
Someone asked him,
"What are you seeking?"
Answer: While he was searching for his own body,
a bystander said to him:
While the body remains upon the bed,
one attains meditative concentration therein and no longer perceives the body;
therefore, birth in that realm is classified as "formless" (ārūpya) within the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) system of meditation.
If, as stated in the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra-śāstra*,
"the form of the formless realm is not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas," we shall for now rely on the perspective of the Hīnayāna.
At this time, one correctly cultivates contemplation below to enter the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness;
next, within the sphere of nothingness, one first refutes ancient errors as described in the *Chanmen* (The Gate of Dhyāna).
Question:
Regarding that state of concentration entered by taking a small amount of consciousness belonging to the sphere of nothingness as an object— how is this so?
Answer: Not so.
One should say that at all times it takes only the sphere of nothingness as its object.
As for the statement that there is a slight degree of consciousness:
it is simply because the mental faculty (manas) encounters the object-field of non-existence (ākiṃcanya-dharmālambana),
giving rise to the perception of a slight degree of consciousness.
One does not enter meditative absorption by taking a limited consciousness as an object.
The present text, based on this, proceeds to refute "that which exists" (*sadbhāva*) and "that which has utility" (*upayoga*).
Following the station of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), it next clarifies the station of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Based on the eight noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), the text here is abbreviated;

it should state that the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is like a disease, the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) and the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) are as described [in the full text],
and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is like a thorn.
That it is not mentioned here is because it is provisionally categorized among the tainted (sāsrava) states;

The faculty of wisdom and the power of wisdom—

Question:

There is certainly no one who abandons two [fetters] and passes away without reaching the third;
nor is there anyone who abandons five [fetters] and passes away without reaching the abandonment of the sixth.
This means that because noble ones exert great effort,

What is called the "Great Chapter" (Mahā-varga) refers to three chapters.

If one cuts off [the fetters] up to the second stage, one must necessarily reach the third.

Question:

Answer:
They differ from the three grades because they involve two meanings of severance.
First, the attainment of the fruit.
Second is the transcending of realms.
Because the ninth grade [of affliction] possesses both obstructive results and the capacity to transcend realms,

The sixth [category] exclusively attains the fruit and lacks the sense of transcending a realm;
therefore, the abandonment of the five [categories] necessarily leads to the sixth.
Within the second and third categories, neither of these two meanings exists at all.
It is beyond doubt that the principle of abandoning two [fetters] necessarily entails three;
what is here referred to as "transcending abandonment" refers to the person of "minor transcendence" mentioned in the subsequent text.
Originally abiding in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and not yet having attained the meditative absorption of the form realm (*rūpadhyāna*),

This is called "one who goes from family to family" (kulaṃkula). Because these five categories are the same as the four categories,

Thus they receive the names "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*), "seed," and the designations for those "approaching" (*pratipannaka*) or "abiding in" (*phalastha*) the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
However, the Great Master’s usage follows the old *Vibhāṣā* entirely;

Furthermore, regarding those who go from family to family (*kulaṃkula*),

It is said that humans attain parinirvāṇa after being born in two or three families, or in two or three continents;

From this, it can be known that human life undergoes two or three rebirths at most.
Therefore, those who attain the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) first among humans—
whether by skipping stages (*vyutkrāntaka*) or by gradual progression (*anupūrvaka*)— subsequently sever three or four [remaining] fetters.

for humans, it is the reverse.

In the final birth among the gods, the severing of the remaining fetters is called attaining parinirvāṇa.
The case of those who pass from family to family (*kulaṃkula*) among humans is explained by analogy with this.

There are five types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*).

Fourth is the one without practice (*apravṛtti*).
Having been born in the form realm, they attain parinirvāṇa before long without practicing effortless cultivation (*anābhoga-pratipatti*);

Fifth is the "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas).
Within the realm of form (rūpadhātu), one must pass through the various levels of the four dhyāna heavens before attaining parinirvāṇa.

The remaining characters in the verse refer to the unmixed cultivation (aśaṃkīrṇabhāvanā).

This refers to one who, having already fully practiced the mixed cultivation within the four dhyānas while in the desire realm,

Why is it necessary to refute others and establish one's own position by borrowing from another?

Answer:
It is precisely because it is common to all that it is called "common" (*sādhāraṇa*).

Because the subsequent two cycles are distinct in their duration,

Many people, failing to see this, claim that the general meaning alone is sufficient and ask why it is necessary to borrow from specific [treatises].
This is the Great Master’s comprehensive application of both the sutras and the śāstras.
Those who hold this judgment maintain that while the specific names belong to the distinct stages, they are used to designate the general positions.
Why is this? If these were definitively restricted to the general stages, one should not establish the "position of subduing" (*vītarāga*) prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*).

Therefore, the Northern system was established to demonstrate this to later students.
This allows the differing interpretations of the ancient and modern masters to be clearly seen.
The statement "borrowing from the distinct [teaching]" (借別) correctly clarifies the borrowing of stages;
first, it borrows the names for the beginning and end of the distinct teaching to designate the universal [teaching].
In the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), there are no distinct stages prior to the first bhūmi to discuss;
therefore, one borrows the stages of the internal and external ordinary persons from the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao),

In the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), there are likewise no further stages after the grounds;

therefore, it simply uses the "Cloud of Dharma" (Fayun) and "Buddha Ground" (Fodi) from the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) as names for the ninth and tenth grounds of the Shared Teaching, which are applied flexibly and without fixed distinction.

If it were a distinct stage, how could that which precedes the "Far-Going" (*dūramgamā*) belong to the two vehicles? This is precisely the same principle as the recent interpretation of the stages, wherein the subduing of afflictions prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) is exactly this case.
If one borrows the subsequent stage, the name "separate ten stages" applies generally to all ten stages;

There was a bhikṣuṇī named Utpalavarṇā.
She was constantly called a prostitute by others;
wishing to remove this ill repute, she transformed herself into a Wheel-Turning King,
possessing the seven treasures and a thousand sons.
When the multitude saw this, they all vacated their seats.
When the transformed king saw the Buddha, he returned to his original form and,
as a bhikṣuṇī, was the very first to pay homage to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the nun:
"It was not you who first paid homage to me;
it was Subhūti alone who first paid homage to me."
Why is this? Subhūti, by contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena, one perceives the Dharma-body;
this constitutes true worship, the most excellent among all forms of worship.
Offering to the physical body is not what is called making an offering.
